records.rationale: An identity-key change creates a recipient-substitution risk before the application prepares ciphertext. Comparing the accepted subject to a locally anchored prior subject, recording the transition, and requiring a fresh independent verification prevent an untrusted directory update, including a later return to the old fingerprint, from silently inheriting trusted status.

A hash chain detects rewritten journal entries but cannot detect that an attacker restored an earlier complete prefix. A separate monotonic trusted head must therefore be checked and updated durably on every accepted change; otherwise valid historic state can falsely authorize new content after a key replacement.

A security notice that exists only in an internal event log is insufficient when users rely on displayed verification status. Accessibility, display ordering, crash consistency and host transaction serialization are necessary to prevent hidden or racing identity changes from being represented as trusted delivery.

A queued message is an authorization to encrypt for a specific observed identity state, not for an arbitrary future account occupant. Binding the queue item to a fingerprint and monotonically increasing journal revision forces renewed user authorization after all transitions, even if the fingerprint cycles back to its original value.

Recovery guess resistance is determined by the real hardware release gate, policy identity and finite attempt budget, not merely the apparent entropy of a user secret. A failed guess must reserve a counter slot before key release so a compromised front end cannot test unlimited candidates and then decide not to count failures.

Counter reset by snapshots, replicas or support channels permits offline-style dictionary attacks through repeated online guesses. The backend must authenticate initiators before any reservation while preserving an explicit denial-of-service model for a malicious already-authorized actor who exhausts the finite budget.

A textual attestation identifier or boolean can be fabricated by the service it purports to constrain. Hardware roots, approved measurements, policy and revocation must be independently verified at the secret-release boundary, including tests that intentionally substitute stale hardware identities and measurements.

Per-replica counters are not a global guess budget: an attacker can multiply attempts across cloned hosts or new replicas. Hardware-backed single-device enforcement or a genuinely strongly consistent shared counter must authorize every release, and replica enrollment must preserve remaining attempts.

Checking counter state and only afterwards incrementing it creates a time-of-check/time-of-use window for repeated guesses. An atomic reservation plus independently trusted checkpoint is required before decryption, with fail-closed handling for network partitions, commit uncertainty and replayed signed snapshots.

Recovery-budget replenishment should be an explicit new authorization event rather than a consequence of elapsed time or an operator button. Separate reset credentials, counter-epoch increments and denial of implicit support privileges preserve the finite-guess guarantee and make malicious exhaustion recoverable only under the chosen policy.

A schema-valid budget receipt demonstrates only that reported fields are internally consistent; it does not prove that an HSM actually enforced the limit. Requiring independently authenticated counter and attestation inputs prevents a reference evaluator from being mistaken for an operating cryptographic release mechanism.

Bounded prekey publication limits exposure and gives operators a testable freshness policy, but the chosen seven-day and thirty-day values are application policy, not a theorem from a cryptographic protocol. Separately limiting retained private keys prevents the nominal public lifetime from concealing a longer decryptability window.

A malicious directory or skewed clock can substitute a future, expired or differently signed prekey bundle and trick a client into an outdated or unauthenticated session. Authenticating the bundle against the intended identity and rejecting ambiguous time and stale offline state prevent insecure availability fallbacks.

One-time keys only contribute their intended replay properties when selected, marked consumed and deleted according to the actual protocol. Quietly skipping stocked keys or endlessly reusing last-resort material increases replay and compromise exposure, so the application must track exhaustion and explicitly disclose delivery tradeoffs.

A classical X3DH profile has no ML-KEM input and must not be mislabeled a broken PQXDH configuration. Conversely, a PQXDH client that accepts missing or substituted PQ material as a classical fallback loses the very protection it advertises, making explicit algorithm and parameter pinning necessary.

An observed server rotation event or new public prekey cannot prove erasure of private material held by the client, its backups or an attacker. Exposure-bound claims therefore depend on device-storage and backup lifecycle evidence, including delayed delivery and old-key grace, not merely metadata freshness.

Push notification payload modes have different attacker-visible content. Wake-only data may still reveal timing and routing, while encrypted-payload mode is confidential only to the chosen endpoint key and cannot treat provider-controlled encryption as E2EE; both modes must declare their remaining observables.

Silent fallback from endpoint-encrypted notifications to provider-decryptable data bypasses the protected recipient set. Explicit mode, allowable outer fields, recipient identity and version checks are required to reject downgrade and unrecognized payload extensions at the final network egress point.

A reused routing token or highly correlated notification timing can join otherwise separate application identities. Scoped identifiers and source-bound observation reporting reduce unnecessary linkage, while avoiding unsupported anonymity guarantees against observers that can correlate global traffic patterns.

A response-delay or batching policy is meaningful only if final dispatch actually enforces it. A digest of a correlation study does not establish a concrete anonymity set, so privacy claims must be limited to the studied observer, service conditions and empirical evidence rather than inferred from policy labels.

Reference policy checking is valuable for rejecting malformed push declarations but cannot establish what bytes a real provider receives or whether the provider holds the decryption key. Product-level privacy therefore needs network captures, endpoint instrumentation and key-control evidence across retries, crashes and notification extensions.

If the responder's first encrypted reply reused initialization key material, an attacker who replays or reflects the initial message could induce nonce or key reuse and recover plaintext relationships. Rejecting known replays and seeding fresh ratchet state ties the first response to a unique, protocol-defined key schedule.

X3DH and the classical Double Ratchet rely only on elliptic-curve assumptions, so recorded traffic is exposed to a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer. Forbidding PQ claims on this profile stops marketing or conformance output from implying harvest-now-decrypt-later protection that the construction cannot provide.

This list is the minimum construction contract for a pairwise session: device-bound identities, authenticated prekeys, the exact named ratchet, per-message keys, authenticated headers, replay rejection, deletion of superseded secrets and fail-closed behaviour. Omitting any one item silently removes a property (authentication, forward secrecy or downgrade resistance) that other claims depend on.

KDF info strings are the only thing separating keys derived for different protocols or purposes from the same secret. An explicit, sufficiently long, protocol-specific constant prevents cross-protocol key reuse where a key derived for one context could be accepted or exploited in another.

A conformance claim is only meaningful if each security-relevant step (exact versions and algorithms, signed-prekey and identity binding, one-time-prekey consumption, AD binding, replay rejection, ratchet initialization, unique keys, deletion) is demonstrated by evidence rather than asserted. Enumerating the evidence prevents a passing interoperability test from standing in for the security checks it never exercised.

Reusing a message key across two AEAD-protected messages can break confidentiality and integrity (nonce reuse) and destroys per-message forward secrecy, since compromise of one key then exposes several messages. Uniqueness must be enforced by the ratchet construction, not by sender behaviour alone.

In SPQR/Triple Ratchet the classical and post-quantum ratchets jointly provide the claimed properties; dropping either changes the security argument (losing PQ protection or classical healing) while keeping the same label. Requiring a different profile for any such change keeps claims tied to the construction actually running.

Free-form protocol names let two implementations believe they speak the same protocol while running different revisions. Restricting identifiers to the versioned pairwise protocol registry makes the selected construction exact, comparable across endpoints and checkable by conformance tooling.

The SPQR security analysis applies to the specific ML-KEM Braid SCKA. Substituting another sparse continuous key agreement under the same profile reference would carry over claims that were never analysed for the substitute, so a different SCKA must be a different, separately reviewed profile.

External protocol documents evolve; if an E2EESA identifier tracked the latest revision, peers on different revisions would claim the same identifier yet be incompatible or have different security properties. Freezing meaning per identifier and requiring a new one for material changes preserves exact interoperability and auditability.

A malicious or compromised service can serve a one-time prekey twice or replay an initial message to reuse key material. Because the service is outside the trust boundary, the endpoint itself must detect replay and prevent key reuse as the selected protocol specifies.

An algorithm marked prohibited has a known break or unacceptable weakness. Permitting its selection, even through negotiation or legacy configuration, would let an attacker or misconfiguration downgrade the session below the minimum the registry allows.

The pairwise policy must name its exact KDF, AEAD and (for PQXDH) post-quantum KEM from the registry. Leaving any primitive implicit lets implementations choose different or weaker components while claiming the same profile, undermining interoperability and the confidentiality argument.

A key directory run by the service can substitute its own key for a recipient device to mount a man-in-the-middle attack. The key-to-device binding must therefore come from authenticated identity/device state and, where deployed, verified transparency or verification views, not from the service's assertion.

Asynchronous messaging requires the responder's prekeys to be available while it is offline, so the service is allowed to host them. This is acceptable only because prekeys are signed and authenticated by the initiator; the permission does not extend trust in the service to the keys' authenticity.

If a failed PQ-capable handshake automatically retried with a classical profile, any network attacker or service could strip post-quantum protection simply by interfering with the first attempt. Refusing automatic weaker retries makes downgrade require explicit policy authorisation instead.

A revoked device may be lost, stolen or compromised. Continuing to establish sessions with it or to encrypt new content to it would deliver plaintext to the attacker holding it, so revocation must take effect for both new sessions and subsequent content.

The X3DH/PQXDH identity key authenticates the session cryptographically, while E2EESA authorization is defined at the device level. Without a cryptographic binding between them, a valid-looking session could terminate at a key that is not an authorized device of the intended identity.

Skipped message keys are needed for out-of-order delivery, but a peer or network attacker can advertise huge counter jumps to exhaust memory or retain many decryption keys, weakening forward secrecy. A configured finite bound makes both resource use and the key-retention window predictable.

PQXDH authenticates parties with classical identity keys and signatures, so an active quantum adversary could impersonate a peer even though harvested traffic remains confidential. Excluding SP-PQ-AUTHENTICATION prevents the PQ KEM component from being mistaken for post-quantum authentication.

End-to-end encryption means the relay and storage service are untrusted for content. The service may handle prekeys and ciphertext for availability, but it must never hold data sufficient to derive message plaintext; otherwise the system is server-side encryption under another name.

The reference checker verifies associated-data byte layout and digest anchors only, so a pass shows structural consistency with PQXDH R3 and ML-KEM Braid but not that signatures or KEM operations were correct. Prohibiting interoperability or cryptographic-verification claims from a structural pass prevents tooling output from being overstated.

Including both identity keys in the associated data binds every ratchet message to the authenticated parties; omitting them enables unknown-key-share or identity-misbinding attacks where a message accepted by one party is attributed to a different peer.

SPQR heals only when public-ratchet progress actually completes, and dropped or withheld messages delay that progress. A claim of continuous post-compromise healing would mislead users after a compromise, so claims must state the sparse, delivery-dependent nature of PQ healing.

Forward secrecy holds only if past keys are actually unrecoverable after an endpoint compromise. Retaining used message keys or superseded chain, root or epoch secrets lets an attacker who later seizes device state decrypt earlier traffic.

An unverified signed prekey lets the service or a network attacker substitute its own prekey and sit in the middle of the initial handshake. Verifying the classical and, where present, the post-quantum signed-prekey bindings before acceptance anchors the session to the responder's identity key.

Properties such as forward secrecy or post-compromise security are only meaningful relative to a threat, a time window and healing conditions. Requiring the structured claim model prevents unqualified labels that overstate protection outside the analysed conditions.

Silent profile changes are the mechanism of downgrade attacks. Requiring changes to be explicit, policy-authorized, bound into the negotiation transcript and recorded for conformance makes any weakening detectable and attributable.

One-time prekeys give the initial message forward secrecy even if the signed prekey is later compromised and limit replay of the first message. Using an available one-time prekey and deleting its private part after consumption preserves those guarantees.

PQXDH with the classical Double Ratchet gives post-quantum confidentiality for the initial key agreement only; subsequent healing is classical. A PQ claim must state its quantum threat model and must not imply PQ authentication or PQ post-compromise healing that the construction lacks.

Retaining initial-message identifiers allows replay detection but creates a durable record of who contacted whom. Permitting such state only under the metadata-minimization rules keeps replay protection from becoming an unbounded relationship log.

Sesame tracks per-device sessions but has its own notion of active devices. If it could add or keep devices independently of the authoritative E2EESA device set, a removed or service-injected device would still receive content; session management must follow, not override, authorization.

A revoked device is presumed lost or compromised. If it stays in group epochs or new content is sent before the removal transition completes, the attacker holding it continues to read group traffic; revocation must therefore propagate into every group and complete before further protected sends.

Changing group profile (for example from MLS to Sender Keys) changes which compromise and membership properties hold. Making such changes explicit, policy-authorized and recorded keeps a weaker profile from being adopted unnoticed and lets assessors see which construction protected which period.

Sender-key rotation after removal exists precisely so the removed device cannot decrypt future messages. Distributing the replacement sender state to a removed device would nullify the rotation and give it continued read access.

MLS, Sender Keys and pairwise fanout have different post-compromise and membership guarantees. A delivery service able to make the preferred profile fail could force a weaker one if fallback were automatic, so fallback must never be triggered by network or service failure alone.

Pairwise fanout provides group confidentiality only if every current recipient device actually received its own valid pairwise ciphertext. Evidence must show one per device so a missing or extra recipient cannot hide behind an aggregate success report.

The delivery service can delay, duplicate or reorder messages and present stale group state. If endpoints relied on it to suppress replays or old epochs, a malicious service could replay content or roll members back; endpoint-side replay and rollback checks are required.

Pairwise fanout's security reduces to the pairwise profile only when each member device gets an independently protected copy. Reusing one ciphertext or a shared key across recipients would introduce a group key outside the analysed pairwise construction.

Sender-key symmetric chains authenticate only group membership, not which member sent a message; any holder could forge another sender's message. Verifying the per-epoch sender signature restores attribution to the specific sending device.

Application membership policy is only enforceable if each transition proves it came from someone the prior state recognises as eligible. Cryptographically verified authorisation rooted in the previous state stops the service or an outsider from fabricating adds or removals.

MLS 1.0 and sender-key groups use classical key schedules; a PQXDH pairwise channel used for distribution does not make the group key PQ-secure. Group PQ claims need a reviewed group construction covering every key path, otherwise harvested group traffic is overclaimed as quantum-safe.

Sender-key chains are static secrets per member; after any membership change both departing members (who know old chains) and new members must be accounted for. Rotating every active sender's state and distributing it only to the new membership over pairwise E2EE is what provides removal and join confidentiality.

Sender-key forward secrecy comes solely from one-way chain advancement with deletion of used keys. Without both, a later compromise of the device exposes all messages still derivable from the retained chain position.

The standard assumes the delivery service is an active adversary for ordering and availability. Stating these capabilities explicitly makes clear that the group design must remain secure against reordering, duplication, withholding and split views rather than relying on honest delivery.

If application data were sent before a Remove commit applied, or the UpdatePath still derived secrets the removed leaf can compute, the removed member would read new-epoch content. Completing removal first and excluding the leaf from path secrets enforces the removal boundary.

The classic attack on server-managed groups is a 'ghost' device silently added by the provider or under legal compulsion. Membership must require cryptographic authorisation the server cannot produce alone, so the service cannot extend the recipient set to itself.

Broadcast semantics imply every current member device (other than the sender) can read a message. Sending to a different set either leaks content to non-members or silently excludes members; equality with the current membership is the checkable definition of correct delivery scope.

Each listed Commit condition closes a known gap: unauthenticated commits allow forgery, skipped epochs allow fork confusion, unauthorised application membership bypasses policy, a missing UpdatePath delays PCS, reused KeyPackages weaken added-member keys, and missing Welcomes leave members stranded. E2EESA tightens base RFC 9420 here deliberately.

An epoch that advanced by more than one or that did not bind subsequent content to the new membership would allow content to be encrypted under a state members never agreed on. Exact single-step advance with binding to the resulting membership keeps all members' views consistent.

The delivery service legitimately routes, stores and orders group traffic. The architecture must ensure these operational capabilities never translate into plaintext access or authority to change membership, keeping the service outside the trust boundary.

Database rows, admin APIs and support tooling are exactly the paths an insider, compromised operator or legal order would use. Treating them as sufficient for membership would reduce E2EE to access control by the provider, so cryptographic authorisation from members is required.

Delayed old-epoch messages can legitimately arrive after removal. If such ciphertext were accepted as belonging to the new epoch, a removed member could inject content that appears current; old ciphertext must remain bound to its original epoch.

A sender-key chain only ratchets forward; anyone who captured its current state can derive all future keys until explicit rotation. Claiming automatic post-compromise security would mislead users into trusting a channel that remains compromised.

MLS cipher suites combine KEM, AEAD, hash and signature choices with different strength. Pinning the exact suite in policy prevents negotiation down to a weaker suite and makes conformance results apply to a known construction.

Every security decision about a group (who may read, which keys apply, whether a message is current) depends on identifying the state precisely. A stable identifier, monotonic epoch, exact membership, profile/version and bound identity state make that state comparable across members and detectably inconsistent when forked.

Sender-key groups combine a KDF, AEAD, signature scheme and a pairwise distribution channel. Leaving any of them unselected allows implementations to diverge or pick weak components while advertising the same group profile.

Without binding group id, epoch, sender identity, chain position and algorithm identifiers, a valid ciphertext could be replayed into another group, another epoch or attributed to another sender. Binding these into AEAD data or the signature makes such cross-context reuse fail authentication.

Requiring the new epoch to be exactly the previous plus one makes skipped or duplicated epochs immediately detectable, preventing a service from creating parallel histories with gaps that members cannot reconcile.

Group security comprises many separable obligations (authorisation, exact membership sets, monotonic epochs, join and removal exclusion, revocation-driven rekey, profile-specific rotation, replay rejection). Requiring demonstration of each prevents a working chat from being presented as evidence of properties it never tested.

Treating a proposal or queued rotation as if it were applied lets a sender encrypt to a membership the group never actually keyed, either leaking to removed devices or excluding new ones. Deriving recipients only from an authenticated applied transition bound to a non-rollbackable anchor closes that gap.

The reference evaluator checks receipt structure and membership consistency but not signatures, Commit authentication or storage durability. Requiring hosts to verify those independently prevents a structural pass from being treated as proof of a secure epoch change.

Stale transitions can re-add removed members, replayed messages can duplicate actions, and epoch-mismatched messages can carry content outside the agreed state. Rejecting all three at the endpoint keeps the accepted group state authoritative against a misbehaving service.

Sending to only part of a group while reporting full-group delivery misrepresents who can read the content and corrupts delivery evidence. Modelling subgroups as their own cryptographic recipient scope keeps evidence and user expectations aligned with the real key distribution.

Retaining skipped keys supports out-of-order delivery but each retained key weakens forward secrecy and consumes memory. An explicit finite maximum prevents a sender or service from forcing unbounded retention.

Sender-key security depends on rotation, authenticated pairwise redistribution, chain advancement, deletion, signatures and skip bounds together; a gap in any one undermines removal confidentiality, forward secrecy or sender authenticity. Evidence must cover each mechanism explicitly.

Each group profile has different FS/PCS behaviour and none provides PQ group authentication; join and removal exclusion also cannot retract content already seen. Constraining claims per profile prevents overstatement, especially the common error of crediting Sender Keys with healing or a PQ distribution path with PQ group security.

Group membership is the point where a device starts receiving content. Requiring prior identity/device authorisation ensures only devices the account owner approved, and not service-injected or unenrolled devices, can join the cryptographic group.

A newly added device should not, by default, gain access to conversation history it was not present for. Excluding it from prior-epoch keys keeps join confidentiality and forces any history access through a separate, explicit capability.

Removal is meaningful only if future keys are independent of anything the removed device held. Establishing fresh keying state that cannot be derived from the prior group state is the cryptographic mechanism behind removal confidentiality.

In pairwise fanout each copy is a separate pairwise message; without binding group id, epoch and group message id into associated data, a copy could be replayed into another group or epoch or presented as a different group message.

These MLS-specific mechanisms carry its security: Commit authentication prevents forged state changes, the required UpdatePath provides healing, single-use KeyPackages protect joiners and Welcomes deliver correct state. Evidence must demonstrate each rather than infer them from successful messaging.

Re-encrypting old content to new members deliberately undoes join confidentiality. Keeping it a separate, explicitly authorised capability prevents ordinary membership operations from silently granting history access.

Group members need to know which authorised device sent a message to act on it safely; anonymous group-key authenticity lets any member impersonate another. Attribution to an authorised sender within the selected architecture prevents intra-group forgery.

Administrative roles and voting rules are application concerns, and the standard deliberately permits them. They remain safe only because transitions still require cryptographic authorisation; this permission defines policy freedom without delegating authority to the service.

A log operator can show each client a different, internally consistent tree (a partition) so that no single client sees a fork. Fork detection must therefore use a channel the operator cannot target per user, such as anonymous log access or gossip of authenticated tree heads.

Third-party-managed deployments shift primary consistency checking to the independent party, so mandatory client checkpoints are relaxed. Clients that do keep state still gain rollback detection at low cost, which is why continuity checking remains recommended.

Each proof element defends a different attack: VRF proofs stop label substitution, commitment openings bind the value, search/greatest-version proofs stop hiding newer keys, inclusion/consistency proofs tie the result to the signed tree, and the subject-digest mapping ties KT output to the identity being verified. A lookup missing any check can be satisfied by a malicious directory.

All KT guarantees derive from the signed tree head; accepting an unsigned or wrongly-keyed head lets anyone fabricate a tree. Verifying the head under the key and configuration of the selected deployment mode anchors every subsequent proof.

A threshold below a strict majority lets a minority of colluding or compromised managers sign conflicting tree heads, so two disjoint quorums could each certify a different view. A strict majority ensures any two valid quorums intersect.

Each listed failure means the directory's claim about a key is unproven or contradicted. Reporting automatic verification as successful in any of these states would give users false assurance precisely when a key substitution or fork may be under way.

KT proves only that some value is consistently published under a label. Unless the authenticated value matches the exact identity subject digest the client expects, a consistent log entry for a different or stale key could be accepted as verification of the current one.

Changing the KT cipher suite mid-log would make prior proofs incomparable and could allow downgrade to a weaker VRF or hash. Fixing it per log configuration and recording it in evidence keeps verification reproducible.

Identity verification and KT must agree on what is being verified. If KT defined its own subject encoding, a manual comparison and a KT proof could refer to different byte strings, letting an attacker satisfy one while violating the other.

The tree is visible to auditors and possibly the public. VRF-concealed labels prevent enumeration of who has accounts, and commitments hide values from parties without the opening, so transparency does not become a directory-harvesting or key-enumeration service.

As with managers, auditors signing under a threshold below a strict majority could produce two non-intersecting approving sets for conflicting views. A majority threshold over independent auditors guarantees overlap and therefore detection.

A tree head far in the future can pre-commit a malicious state; one far in the past can freeze a client on an old view that hides key changes. Enforcing bounded skew in both directions limits freshness attacks.

KT publishes state; it does not authorise it. Publishing a key that the identity architecture has not already accepted would make the log a channel for introducing unauthorised keys that then appear legitimate.

Gossip only detects partitions if honest users form a connected graph; sparse or isolated gossip leaves targeted users unprotected. Prohibiting global-consistency claims from occasional exchange keeps the claim aligned with the real detection guarantee.

The reference validator checks semantic results that someone else already verified; it cannot detect a forged proof. Requiring a conformant implementation of the pinned protocol for the actual cryptography prevents the semantic layer from being mistaken for proof verification.

Without retained authenticated state, a client cannot distinguish a legitimate new tree from a rolled-back or forked one between cycles. Persisting checkpoints is what turns individual proofs into continuity guarantees.

Auditor-backed results are only as strong as the auditors' coverage. Too few attestations, excessive lag, an auditor that began after the relied-upon state, or conflict with client state each means the independent check does not actually cover what the client trusts.

Treating a later observation without its required checkpoint as a first observation would discard the continuity check, letting an attacker erase or omit stored state to bypass rollback and fork detection.

In third-party profiles the independent party detects forks, but adding gossip or anonymous comparison provides defence in depth if that party fails or colludes. The permission allows layering without weakening the primary mechanism.
Contact monitoring checks that the looked-up key remains consistent over time. Treating a lookup as fully monitored before that operation completes would present a partial guarantee as complete.

After state loss, rollback and fork detection are no longer possible until recovery conditions are met. Signalling degraded assurance prevents users from relying on verification that silently lost its continuity basis.

If cryptographic failures look like connectivity errors, users and operators dismiss them as transient and miss an attack. Distinguishing them lets security failures be investigated rather than retried.

If clients lose state more often than the monitoring window or auditor lag, an attacker can time a malicious change so it is never checked against retained state. Requiring the windows to be materially shorter than expected state-loss intervals keeps detection meaningful.

A third-party profile's security depends on how many independent parties exist, how many must sign, how stale their view may be and whether clients persist checkpoints. Leaving any parameter unspecified makes the guarantee undefined.

KT verification and a manual safety-number comparison provide different assurance: KT relies on log and monitoring assumptions, manual comparison on an out-of-band channel. Labelling a KT result as manual verification would overstate what the user actually did.

Checkpoints in volatile or easily replaced storage can be deleted or rolled back by malware or an attacker with device access, defeating continuity checks. Durable, rollback-resistant storage preserves the reference point.

Third parties sharing an operator, hosting provider or network can fail or be compelled together, collapsing an apparent threshold into a single point. Independent failure domains make the threshold meaningful.

When a separate manager runs the tree, the service operator is the party best placed to notice the manager presenting different views. Requiring a fork-detection mechanism on the operator side prevents a manager equivocating unobserved.

Inclusion proves publication, not legitimacy: a compromised account or service could publish an attacker key. Inclusion must not substitute for identity-architecture authorisation, otherwise transparency launders unauthorised keys.

Committing to the exact subject digest ensures the published value refers unambiguously to one identity/key subject. Committing to anything looser would allow different keys to share a published value or verification to apply to the wrong subject.

Freshness bounds are meaningless unless the head's timestamp is compared to the client's own observation time. This comparison is what detects stale or pre-dated heads used to freeze or front-run clients.

The core purpose of key transparency is to stop a directory showing different keys to different users for long periods without detection. This requirement states that goal relative to the selected profile's assumptions so it can be tested and its limits stated.

Each rejection condition represents a concrete attack: forged heads, future-dating, stale views, shrinking trees (rollback) and same-size different-root forks. Rejecting all of them is the minimum for tree-head acceptance to imply consistency.

The pinned KT specification is an Internet-Draft that may change incompatibly. Treating a later draft as equivalent would let peers using different semantics believe they interoperate and inherit unreviewed security changes; material changes need a new identifier.
In manager-based modes the manager's authentication of the tree state is what binds it to an accountable party. Skipping this check would allow anyone in the path to supply a fabricated state.

Only the label owner knows which keys it legitimately published. Owner monitoring detects unauthorised new versions, hidden prior versions or out-of-order updates that no other party can recognise as illegitimate.
A conformance result implies the owner is watching for unauthorised changes. If monitoring has lapsed, presenting the result as current overstates protection; failure must block that representation.
This formula is the concrete strict-majority rule for third-party thresholds, ensuring any two valid signing sets overlap so conflicting views cannot both be certified.
Where the protocol requires operator authorisation of label updates, verifying it ensures only operator-approved updates enter the tree and gives a signed record attributing each change.

An unsalted hash of a phone number or email is trivially reversible by enumeration, turning the public tree into a user directory. VRF labels require the operator's private key to compute, preserving label privacy.

A threshold larger than the number of third parties can never be met, causing either permanent failure or implementations quietly bypassing the check. Bounding it by the count keeps the policy satisfiable and enforced.

Owner monitoring only helps if it actually runs; manual monitoring is rarely performed. Automatic background monitoring where feasible makes detection of unauthorised key publication the default rather than an opt-in.

A verification result is only auditable if the exact profile, protocol, subject, version, tree state, individual proof results, checkpoint and monitoring state are preserved. Without this evidence an assessor cannot reproduce or challenge a claimed successful verification.

Services may legitimately restrict who can search or update labels, for example to limit enumeration. The permission is conditional on still meeting monitoring requirements so access control cannot be used to block owners or monitors from detecting misbehaviour.

A syntactically valid response says nothing about whether the key is consistent with what others see. Accepting it without proof verification reduces KT to trusting the service, which is exactly the threat KT exists to counter.

A consistency proof from the retained checkpoint shows the new tree is an append-only extension of the old one. Without it, the operator could rewrite history between observations and the client would not notice.

A safety number is only useful if it represents the keys the system will actually use. Deriving snapshots from already-accepted identity state, rather than from whatever the service reports, prevents users verifying keys that are not the authorised ones.

Verification attests to a specific set of keys. Silently carrying the verified flag to a new subject would make a substituted key look verified, which is exactly the attack verification exists to expose.
Safety numbers depend on a collision-resistant hash; a prohibited hash could allow an attacker to construct a different key set with the same displayed value, defeating manual comparison.

If the numeric and QR forms were computed from different inputs, users could successfully compare one while the other covered different keys. A single subject digest guarantees both forms verify the same thing.

A verification record must let the product later determine exactly what was verified, how, and under which profile. Preserving profile, hash, identities, full digest, displayed values, method and explicit confirmation makes invalidation decisions and audits possible.

Messages queued before a recipient's identity changed were authorised against the old keys. Re-evaluating them before delivery prevents content composed for a verified peer being sent to a possibly substituted one.

Verification is a unilateral act by one user. Implying that the peer also verified would give each side false confidence about the other's assurance; only explicit end-to-end synchronisation may share that state.

Stored verification is only valid if the subject has not changed since. Recomputing the canonical subject from current accepted state before relying on the record is the check that detects intervening key changes.

If the two parties used different profiles their subjects would differ and comparison would always fail, or worse, implementations might reconcile differences loosely. Requiring the same pinned profile makes the comparison well-defined.

A precisely specified, versioned QR format with canonical content ensures scanners interpret payloads identically and cannot be fooled by alternative encodings. The prefix and fields bind version, profile, hash, identities and full digest.
A key list from the service that has not passed device authorisation could include attacker-injected keys. Treating it as a snapshot would let users 'verify' a man-in-the-middle configuration.
Key transparency proves directory consistency, not that the account belongs to a particular person. Representing it as real-world identity proof would mislead users about impersonation risk.
Verified status asserts that the current keys were compared out of band. Once the verified subject changes that assertion is false; keeping the badge would hide a possible key substitution.

These demonstrations cover deterministic subjects, consistent representations, pinning, malformed-input rejection, explicit confirmation, invalidation on change, stability across authorised subordinate changes and refusal of server-created verification. Each targets a distinct failure that would make verification either useless or misleading.

Displaying a code is not verification; the security comes from the user actually comparing it. Recording verification only after affirmative confirmation prevents accidental or automatic 'verified' states.

After a subject change, the previous comparison no longer covers the current keys. Invalidating, surfacing the change and requiring a new comparison ensures users cannot be silently moved from a verified to an unverified peer.

Comparing codes over the same service being verified lets that service alter both sides. An independent channel (in person, trusted call) is what breaks the service's ability to man-in-the-middle the comparison.

If invalidation is not persisted atomically before use, a crash or race could restore the old verified status and let content be sent under stale trust. Durable persistence makes invalidation irreversible except by re-verification.

An attacker might rotate a key away and back to the original. Automatically restoring 'verified' when the old digest reappears would let such a sequence bypass the user's attention; restoration must be a new explicit comparison.
The hash determines collision resistance of the safety number. Selecting it from the registry ensures a reviewed, lifecycle-managed algorithm rather than an ad hoc choice.

In device-set verification, any change to the active keys alters who can decrypt. Every such change must alter the subject and invalidate prior verification so that injected or rotated devices cannot inherit trust.

If the server that might be substituting keys can also declare that the codes matched, verification provides no protection against that server. The match decision must rest with the users' independent comparison.

Lenient QR parsing allows crafted payloads that display as valid while encoding different identities or digests. Strict rejection of unsupported or unexpected content prevents scanner confusion attacks.

Two parties must compute byte-identical subjects to compare them. Canonical sorted UTF-8 JSON without insignificant whitespace removes encoding ambiguity that could make honest comparisons fail or permit two encodings of different data to collide in interpretation.
The account root anchors all device authorisation. A changed root means a different authority now controls the identity, so prior verification of the old root cannot carry over.

Automatic transparency evidence and a human out-of-band comparison carry different assurance. Keeping them distinguishable stops automated checks from being presented as stronger, user-performed verification.
Presenting QR and numeric forms as different checks would confuse users into thinking one is stronger or that both are needed. They encode the same subject, and the UI must reflect that equivalence.

A domain separator prevents subject digests being confused with hashes from other protocols; version and profile fields prevent cross-version collisions; sorting the parties makes the subject identical from both perspectives so each side sees the same code.

Rotation must be observable and ordered: generation plus one detects skipped or replayed rotations, and permanently retiring old keys prevents an attacker who stole a retired key from having it reinstated.

If the service held the account-root private key, it could authorise devices on its own and defeat end-to-end encryption. Keeping the root client-controlled ensures device authorisation reflects the user's decision.

Sequence and preceding-state hash checks make the identity history a hash chain, rejecting forks and replays a peer can see locally. The text notes that global split views still need key transparency, preventing overclaiming of local checks.

Distinct device and key identities let each recipient be authorised, revoked and verified individually. Reusing identifiers would let a revoked device's identity or key be confused with a new one and inherit its trust.

A recovered or replacement endpoint is a new cryptographic party possibly controlled by an attacker who abused recovery. Automatically inheriting peer verification or group membership would let that attacker receive content without peers noticing.

When every device is lost there is no cryptographic authority left, and service-side recovery paths are exactly what attackers abuse for account takeover. Requiring products to choose and disclose an explicit recovery contract makes the resulting trust trade-off visible.

The authoriser field is meaningful only if each signature was checked against a key authorised in the exact preceding state. Populating it earlier would let unverified or stale authorisers appear valid; the note limits the reference evaluator's claim.

Caches of device and membership keys can outlive revocation. Each profile must define how revocation removes the device from future protected state, otherwise cached keys keep encrypting to a revoked device.

Conformance requires a pinned profile, common invariants, fail-closed parsing, refusal of server-only authorisation and both positive and negative transition cases. These together demonstrate that device management cannot be subverted by the service or by malformed input.
Exact sequence and current-state hash bind each event to a single predecessor, so the identity history is linear and tamper-evident; replays, reorderings and forks fail validation.

Recovery creates authority from outside the normal device chain and carries different risk. Making it distinguishable lets peers and policies treat recovered identities with appropriate scrutiny rather than as routine enrollments.

These channels are controlled by the service or by third parties such as email and telephone providers and are frequently hijacked. Allowing them to satisfy cryptographic authorisation would make SIM-swap or support social engineering sufficient to add devices.

If ordinary flows could leave zero active devices, the identity would have no remaining authority and would be forced into weaker recovery paths. Keeping at least one active device preserves the cryptographic chain of control.
Enrolling exactly one fresh device at generation 1 with distinct, never-used keys keeps every device's key history unambiguous and prevents enrollment from smuggling in a reused or shared key.

Duplicate identifiers or fingerprints create ambiguity about which device a key belongs to; reused retired keys reinstate possibly compromised material; wrong-role or prohibited algorithms break cryptographic assumptions. A consumer must reject all of these to keep state well-formed.

Service accounts serve operational purposes, but service credentials are held or resettable by the provider. If they alone could authorise a recipient device, a compromised account or insider could add an eavesdropping device.

Requiring another active device for rotation or revocation prevents a single stolen device from locking out the owner or rotating keys unilaterally, while still letting a sole device rotate its own keys and preventing it from revoking itself into an authority-less state.

In the device-chain profile authority lives only in active devices; without a root key, enrollment must be approved by an existing active device so that new devices cannot appear without an authorised party's consent.

Identity keys must use reviewed algorithms with lifecycle management. Restricting choices to registry identifiers and constraints, and defining no new primitives, keeps identity security grounded in analysed cryptography.

Recovery that changes the device set bypasses ordinary device-approved enrollment. Governing it by the recovery profile ensures its stricter controls and disclosures apply instead of the ordinary rules.
A revoked device is untrusted; allowing it to authorise later transitions would let a stolen device re-enrol itself or others, and keeping it as a recipient would continue leaking content to it.

This is the central E2EE property for device management: no non-recipient party, including the provider, can grant itself decryption capability. Without it, all content protection reduces to provider honesty.

A service can present a fabricated or stale identity history. Endpoints must validate against retained local state or transparency and fail closed on revoked authority or inconsistent history; waiting periods are friction, not cryptographic proof.

Binding identity, event, subject device, sequence, previous-state hash, new keys and verified authorisers into one authenticated event prevents any component being swapped or replayed independently, giving each transition an unambiguous, verifiable meaning.

Replaying an old negotiation could reinstate a previously acceptable but now superseded version, suite or authorisation. Treating repeated contexts as fresh would let an attacker resurrect stale decisions, so replay must be refused where it affects security-relevant selection.

An attacker in the path can easily cause errors. If errors led to a successful but weaker connection, interference would become a downgrade tool; failing closed makes interference cost availability rather than security.

Pinning the registry version and an explicit suite set fixes exactly what may be negotiated, so both peers and assessors know the acceptable options and a peer cannot introduce suites the policy never approved.

Any downgrade-sensitive field not covered by the authenticated transcript can be altered in transit without detection. Failing when coverage is incomplete prevents a partially authenticated negotiation from being trusted.

Aliases, provider defaults and floating references can resolve to different algorithms over time or across libraries. Requiring exact identifiers ensures that a suite pin means the same construction everywhere it is evaluated.

Supporting strong algorithms is irrelevant if an attacker can force the weaker ones. Downgrade resistance is a property of the negotiation mechanism, so the claim must be earned by negotiation behaviour, not by the algorithm list.

Weakening policy to find common ground is precisely what a downgrade attacker wants. Surfacing incompatibility instead keeps policy authoritative and makes the condition visible for deliberate administrative action.

Freshness must make each negotiation unique and bound to its participants. Protocols may use other mechanisms than paired nonces, but only if they provide equivalent uniqueness and authenticated binding, preventing cross-session replay.

Version strings do not reliably encode security order (e.g. '1.10' vs '1.9', or vendor suffixes). Inferring order from comparison could select a weaker version as 'highest'; the explicit policy order must be used.

Protocols may authenticate more fields for their own needs, but removing a baseline field reopens the specific tampering that field's binding prevented. Policies can extend, never shrink, the baseline.

If an intermediary could shift the effective profile set without producing a distinct authenticated outcome, both sides might believe they agreed on stronger profiles than were applied. Each profile set must map to its own authenticated result.

Administrators legitimately change policy, but such changes carry accountability. Distinguishing them from automatic fallback ensures weakening is always a recorded human decision and never disguised as negotiation.
A minimum version exists to exclude versions with known weaknesses. Negotiating below it whenever nothing better is shared would make the floor advisory; failing enforces it.

Each demonstration targets a specific downgrade vector: floors, highest-version choice, suite pinning, transcript coverage, registry binding, fallback suppression, adversarial downgrade attempts and replay. Requiring them prevents a product from claiming negotiation safety while testing only the happy path.
Binding the exact effective profile set ties the connection's security claims to what was actually evaluated, so no party can later assert that different, stronger profiles applied.
An explicit oldest-to-newest order and minimum version give negotiation an unambiguous definition of 'stronger' and 'acceptable', removing reliance on heuristics or string comparison.
Selecting the highest mutually supported version prevents an attacker or lazy implementation from settling on an older version both sides could have avoided.

Cryptographic agility is needed for migration but historically has been the root of many downgrade attacks (export ciphers, version rollback). Stating that agility must not enable downgrade frames all other negotiation rules.

The listed rejection conditions make the reference validator detect every evidence pattern that indicates a downgrade or replay: non-highest or sub-floor versions, unpinned or non-mutual suites, pin mismatches, unauthenticated fields, attempted fallback and bad freshness.

Choosing a suite that one party did not authentically advertise means either tampering occurred or the selection is unilateral. Requiring presence in both authenticated sets ensures the result is genuinely mutual.

Each listed retry behaviour is a known way a failure becomes a downgrade: lowering the floor, dropping strong versions, adding weak suites, changing profiles or registry, or disabling binding. Forbidding automatic retries along these axes prevents attacker-induced failures from weakening security.
Connection success is not a security goal that overrides policy. An endpoint accepting anything weaker or different than its pin to make a connection work would let any peer dictate weaker terms.

Advertising, selecting or accepting an unpinned suite at any step widens the attack surface beyond policy. Enforcing the pinned set at all three points closes every route by which a non-approved suite could be used.

Without protocol-level freshness, an authenticated transcript from an earlier session could be replayed to reproduce an old outcome. Binding to freshness makes every negotiation result session-specific.

Ranking suites by strength would embed contestable judgements and could push deployments toward unsuitable choices. Leaving ranking to later profiles while keeping pinning and transcript binding mandatory preserves downgrade resistance without false precision.

Binding the complete offered and supported sets, policy, protocol, registry and selections before application traffic lets each side detect any modification of the other's offer, which is how version-rollback and suite-stripping attacks are caught.

ALPN selects the application protocol carried over TLS. Accepting an unpermitted protocol enables cross-protocol attacks where a client of one service is redirected to another endpoint sharing the certificate; restricting to policy-listed protocols prevents that confusion.
TLS 1.2 and earlier permit non-forward-secret key exchange, weaker transcript protection and known downgrade issues. Restricting to TLS 1.3 removes those legacy modes from the attack surface.
Without chain validation to a configured trust anchor, any self-issued certificate could impersonate the server and the TLS channel would be open to man-in-the-middle interception.

The Common Name is an untyped, legacy field and certificates may contain names unrelated to the intended service. RFC 9525 requires typed subjectAltName identifiers; CN fallback allows certificates never meant for the service to be accepted.

0-RTT data is replayable by a network attacker and lacks full forward secrecy. It is only safe for operations explicitly analysed as replay-tolerant with defined replay protection and early-data rejection handling, so a documented application profile must exist before enabling it.

Exported traffic secrets (e.g. SSLKEYLOGFILE) let anyone with the log decrypt captured traffic. Production must disable export unless a governed diagnostic mode defines authority, audit, protection, retention and restoration.

Each demonstrated item corresponds to a transport property: version, mode, offered and permitted groups, hybrid requirement, obsolete-group exclusion, suite, fresh key share, ALPN and certificate validation. Enumerating them stops a successful connection being taken as proof the secure configuration was negotiated.

Transport security protects hops; application E2EE protects content from the service. A transport component that terminated or weakened the E2EE layer would expose plaintext to infrastructure, collapsing the two layers into one.

Session resumption can skip the original key exchange. If a resumed hybrid session used only classical key agreement it would lose PQ confidentiality while still claiming it; the hybrid group must be renegotiated on resumption.
A terminating proxy decrypts traffic, so TLS through it is not end-to-end between users. Calling it E2EE misleads users about who can read their content.
psk_ke resumption reuses the original secret and loses forward secrecy if the PSK leaks. psk_dhe_ke adds fresh ephemeral agreement, keeping resumed connections forward-secret.

Mutual TLS is meaningful only if the server requests, the client presents, the chain validates and the identity is authorised for the role. Missing any step leaves service-to-service calls accepting unauthenticated or unauthorised clients.

If a hybrid-profile endpoint ended up on a classical-only group but still reported hybrid conformance, monitoring would show PQ protection that was not present. Silent continuation is how downgrades go unnoticed.

Pinning can add protection against mis-issued certificates but causes outages and lockout if keys rotate without a plan. Permitting it only with a rotation and recovery design avoids trading a security gain for an availability failure.
Falling back from hybrid to classical on failure lets an attacker who blocks large ClientHellos strip PQ protection. The hybrid profile must fail instead of continuing under the same claim.
Replayed early data could repeat a payment, permission change or destructive action. Advising against 0-RTT for these operation classes keeps replay risk to idempotent, low-impact requests.

QUIC with TLS 1.3 per RFC 9001 provides the same handshake security as TLS over TCP. Permitting it lets deployments use QUIC without defining a separate security profile, while the same pinning and claims apply.

Inside a mesh, network location is easy to spoof or reach after lateral movement. Exposing the cryptographically authenticated peer identity lets authorisation decisions rely on who the peer is rather than where traffic came from.

Even where an intermediary legitimately terminates TLS, it must not gain access to E2EE-protected content unless it is itself an authorised endpoint. This keeps infrastructure outside the content trust boundary.

Any negotiated parameter outside policy indicates misconfiguration or attack. Failing closed on version, suite, group, ALPN, trust model or authentication mode deviations prevents connections from continuing on unapproved terms.

A valid chain proves the certificate was issued by a trusted CA, not that it was issued for this service. Without matching the expected service identity, any valid certificate for any domain would authenticate the connection.

Resumption reduces latency and load and is safe in TLS 1.3 when combined with fresh ephemeral agreement and the other resumption rules. The permission is conditional on those rules rather than unconditional.
Requiring ALPN makes the application protocol an authenticated part of the handshake, preventing cross-protocol redirection and protocol confusion between services sharing infrastructure.
RFC 9525 defines how to match typed service identifiers and when wildcards apply. Following it avoids the historical inconsistencies in hostname verification that led to certificate-acceptance bugs.

Identity verification needs a precise reference identifier derived from the intended service. Constructing it from user input or redirects without care lets attackers steer clients to accept certificates for other names.
Reusing an ephemeral key share links connections and means one key compromise exposes multiple sessions, weakening forward secrecy. Fresh key shares per connection keep sessions independent.

Hybrid TLS groups protect key exchange against harvest-now-decrypt-later, but server and client authentication still use classical signatures. Claiming PQ authentication would misstate protection against an active quantum attacker.
A profile named hybrid is only meaningful if the connection actually used a hybrid group. Requiring negotiation of a listed group ties the claim to observable handshake behaviour.

Chain validity, service identity and platform CT enforcement answer different questions, and passing one must not imply another. Evaluating them independently, without CN fallback, and without over-applying public CT to private PKI, keeps each check precise.

Hybrid key shares enlarge ClientHellos, which can exceed QUIC amplification limits or path MTU and cause failures. Planning for the size prevents availability problems that might otherwise pressure operators toward classical fallback.
Documenting group sets and preference lets assessors check which key exchanges are possible and whether the preferred group matches the claimed security level.
The traditional profile uses only classical ECDHE, so recorded traffic remains vulnerable to a future quantum computer. Prohibiting PQ confidentiality claims prevents overstatement.

A certificate valid for several services lets an attacker redirect a client of one service to another endpoint that accepts the same identity, enabling cross-protocol attacks. Service-scoped identifiers and ALPN limits contain that risk.

ECH has several states with different privacy implications. Treating a failure as permission to drop ECH lets an on-path attacker trivially disable it; required ECH must reject unprotected fallback and only follow authenticated retry or disable paths.
Without a replay-safety profile no one has decided which operations tolerate replay. Keeping 0-RTT off by default prevents accidental exposure of non-idempotent operations to replay.

The pre-standard Kyber draft code points used an earlier, non-final algorithm and are not the reviewed ML-KEM constructions. Negotiating them would give an unreviewed and possibly incompatible PQ claim.
Draft-Kyber and final ML-KEM groups differ cryptographically; treating them as equivalent would carry claims across constructions. Migration must move to the RFC 10024 groups explicitly.
If a private trust anchor could be delivered over the connection it authenticates, an attacker could supply its own anchor. Independent authenticated provisioning breaks that circularity.
Some service-to-service paths need cryptographic client identity. Permitting mutual TLS as a policy option lets deployments require it where client authentication matters, subject to the mTLS rules.

ECH hides the inner SNI but not IP addresses, DNS, timing or outer fields. Describing its scope accurately, and noting that the reference checker does not prove deployed behaviour, prevents privacy and assurance overclaims.
Expired or not-yet-valid certificates may belong to revoked or retired keys. Enforcing the validity period limits the window in which a compromised certificate can be used.
